claims.text: Anthropic's multi-agent research system with a Claude Opus 4 lead agent and Claude Sonnet 4 subagents outperformed single-agent Claude Opus 4 by 90.2% on Anthropic's internal research evaluation.
In Anthropic's BrowseComp analysis, token usage alone explained 80% of performance variance, and token usage, tool-call count and model choice together explained 95%.
Agents use about 4x the tokens of chat, and multi-agent systems use about 15x the tokens of chat, so Anthropic recommends multi-agent systems only for tasks valuable enough to justify the extra cost.
Parallelism (3-5 concurrent subagents, each making three or more parallel tool calls) reduced research time by up to 90% on complex queries.

Early versions of the research system sometimes spawned 50 subagents for simple questions, searched endlessly for nonexistent sources, and continued after having sufficient information; Anthropic added scaling rules and stopping guidance.

The research system's prompt guidelines set effort budgets: one agent with 3-10 tool calls for simple fact-finding, 2-4 subagents with 10-15 calls each for comparisons, and more than 10 subagents for complex research.

Vague delegation instructions caused duplicate searches, gaps and mismatched scopes; for example, one subagent researched the 2021 chip crisis while others duplicated 2025 supply-chain research. Delegations should specify objective, output format, tool guidance and boundaries.

The research system uses an orchestrator-worker architecture in which a LeadResearcher plans and delegates to subagents, and a CitationAgent later identifies citation locations; the lead saves its plan to external memory because context beyond 200,000 tokens would be truncated.
A tool-testing agent that repeatedly exercised a flawed MCP tool and rewrote its description reduced task completion time by 40%.

The research system's lead agent waits for each batch of subagents to finish, creating a slowest-worker bottleneck; asynchronous execution was identified as an opportunity but brings coordination, state-consistency and error-propagation challenges.
Anthropic used rainbow deployments, running old and new versions simultaneously while gradually shifting traffic, so updates do not interrupt agents mid-run.
Anthropic says tasks with tightly shared context or many dependencies, including most coding work, are poorer fits for multi-agent systems than breadth-first research.

In the long-running harness design, an initializer session creates init.sh, claude-progress.txt and an initial git commit, and subsequent coding agents make incremental progress and leave structured handoffs.

In the Claude.ai-clone example, the initializer produced more than 200 features as a JSON list initially marked failing; coding agents were instructed to change only the passes status, because models were less likely to inappropriately overwrite JSON than Markdown.
Agents were told to implement one feature at a time because attempting the whole application exhausted context mid-implementation and left half-finished work.
Unit tests and curl checks were insufficient to detect broken user workflows; explicit instructions to use browser automation via Puppeteer MCP substantially improved failure detection.

Each coding session begins by checking the working directory, reading progress notes, git history and the feature list, starting the dev server and running a basic end-to-end test, and ends with a descriptive commit and progress update.

Anthropic's September 2025 compaction implementation summarized architectural decisions, unresolved bugs and implementation details, then continued with the summary plus the five most recently accessed files; it recommends tuning for recall first, then precision.
Subagents can explore using tens of thousands of tokens while returning a distilled summary of often 1,000-2,000 tokens to the parent agent.

Sonnet 4.5 showed 'context anxiety', wrapping up prematurely near its perceived context limit, so context resets were needed; Opus 4.5 largely removed this, allowing continuous sessions with automatic compaction.

In a later planner/generator/evaluator harness, one application ran 20 minutes for $9 solo versus 6 hours for $200 with the full harness, and a DAW experiment with Opus 4.6 cost $124.70 and took 3 hours 50 minutes.

Anthropic recommends removing harness components one at a time and inspecting the effects, since a radical simplification failed to reproduce earlier quality and obscured which components were load-bearing.
A non-fork subagent starts fresh without the parent's conversation, tool results or system prompt, so delegations must include relevant context, and only its final message returns to the parent.

Agent Skills use three-stage progressive disclosure: names and descriptions load first, the full SKILL.md loads when relevant, and linked resources load only as needed; Anthropic warns malicious Skills can exfiltrate data or cause unintended actions.

On October 22, 2026, Anthropic announced donating Agent Skills to the Agentic AI Foundation, reporting more than 70 integrating platforms, 1 million published Skills and nearly 280 million installations.
